sessions.summary: A hands-on session about how each of us actually builds with AI day to day. Most of the time went to two themes: running models locally versus paying for cloud models, and showing real working setups. We compared local-model runners and hardware limits, walked through live project builds, and shared workflow tips for keeping AI projects organised and reasonably secure.

topics.title: Local models vs paid cloud
topics.summary: The central debate of the session. Running models locally through Ollama or LM Studio is free and private, but the group agreed it needs serious hardware and still trails the paid cloud models on quality. Justas recommended LM Studio because it shows which models actually fit your machine. Eividas reached for a stronger cloud model (Sonnet via OpenClaw) when a task needed real power. The shared conclusion was a pragmatic mix, use the cheapest tool that is good enough for the job rather than forcing everything local or everything cloud.

topics.title: Hardware and model size
topics.summary: A practical look at what it takes to run the bigger models. Frederik explained that a 32-billion-parameter model needs roughly 40 GB of memory at FP4/FP8 precision, which is why most laptops simply can't run the strong models locally. The group noted that different tasks lean on different hardware, image generation wants a capable GPU, while voice and transcription lean more on the CPU. Eividas summed up the trade-off: local models are free but slower and lower quality than the cloud options.

topics.title: Running local AI tools
topics.summary: How people actually run things on their own machines. Eividas walked through generating images locally with Flux / FLUX.2 [klein] on a home GPU, installed and managed through Pinokio (a one-click installer that pulls in missing dependencies) and ComfyUI for the node-based image workflow. Ollama and LM Studio came up again as the friendlier ways to download and serve local LLMs.

topics.title: Coding agents and IDE setups
topics.summary: The tools the group uses to write code with AI. Cline and Continue run as VS Code extensions, GitHub Copilot gives inline suggestions, and Claude Code was used to build whole projects end to end. Eividas advised sticking to Copilot or other verified plugins when wiring models into VS Code, rather than trusting unknown extensions.

topics.title: Live project builds
topics.summary: The hands-on demos. Auri live-built a small currency-converter web app with Claude Code, added Supabase plus Google sign-in so users never manage a password, and deployed it to Vercel, then toured the community dashboard with its forum and idea-voting. Yogi showed a business operations dashboard built with Claude that pulls in live data through several connected APIs, and mentioned using Whisper to clone his voice and Claude to draft offers and estimates.

topics.title: Workflow, security and staying organised
topics.summary: Tips for keeping AI projects tidy and safe. The group shared working in focused blocks with a Pomodoro timer, capturing notes and transcription in Notion, and double-checking every GitHub push so secrets don't leak by accident. Justas raised the trust question around granting Google auth access and pushing credentials to GitHub.

topics.title: Funding and monetisation
topics.summary: A short thread on keeping a community project sustainable. Auri weighed relying on one large backer against taking many smaller donations, leaning toward smaller contributions to stay independent.

sessions.summary: The session covered various applications of AI tools across different domains such as image generation, business trading, creative projects, project management, design and development, cryptocurrency trading, and gaming. The group discussed specific tools like Mato elements, Adobe Illustrator's AI features, VAE, Blender, and others, focusing on their practical uses and potential benefits

topics.title: AI Tools for Image Generation
topics.summary: The discussion centered around various AI tools used in image generation. Auri highlighted the use of Mato elements, Adobe Illustrator's AI features, and VAE for specific sections of websites. Andrei mentioned the potential of AI in creating 3D models and generating SVG files from vector forms

topics.title: AI in Business and Trading
topics.summary: Participants explored the use of AI in business purposes such as trading platforms and data labeling services. Ignas shared his experience with AI tools like Claude for drawing tasks, emphasizing potential risks associated with small budget trades due to tax issues and increased scrutiny from accountants. He also recommended Koinly for simplifying crypto platform report exports

topics.title: AI in Creative Projects
topics.summary: The group discussed various creative applications of AI, including generating brand guides, creating 3D models with Blender and Fusion, and using AI to enhance presentations. Auri described a presentation tool he built for saving containers as PDFs, while Ignas discussed his efforts to integrate pictures into specific projects without overriding manual changes

topics.title: AI in Project Management
topics.summary: The conversation delved into project management tools with a focus on security and API limitations. Eividas suggested using 'AS' for the project name due to its ease of searchability, while Andrei highlighted the need for better UX design in presentations. The group also touched upon the use of CLAUDE.md for security workflows and design files

topics.title: AI in Design and Development
topics.summary: The discussion included various AI tools used in design and development, such as OpenClaw, Hermes, and Stingy. Andrei mentioned downloading models from Ollama via API URL and the potential of AI to create 3D models for technical purposes. Sany proposed using AI to generate photographs for better fitting visuals

topics.title: AI in Cryptocurrency Trading
topics.summary: The group debated the use of AI in cryptocurrency trading, with Ignas warning about the risks and potential losses associated with small budget trades. He recommended connecting history with trading platforms to avoid increased scrutiny from accountants but noted that accounting costs are high despite providing legal advice

topics.title: AI in Gaming
topics.summary: The discussion included AI applications in gaming, such as recreating GTA Six and using AI for data labeling. Ignas shared his experience with a platform called CrowdSomething where people can label data for free but get paid small amounts. Auri mentioned the use of AI to create brand guides by copying images from new websites

topics.title: How I steer my AI: one CLAUDE.md

flow.label: Write the rules once
flow.detail: Three files: WORKFLOW, SECURITY and DESIGN

flow.label: Point CLAUDE.md at them
flow.detail: A short global file that links the three

flow.label: Read on every session
flow.detail: The AI loads them before it touches any project

flow.label: Standards enforced
flow.detail: Security, git flow and design stay consistent

files.name: CLAUDE.md
files.does: The index the AI reads first. A short global file that points to the other three.

rules.rule: Who I am and how to talk to me: be direct, recommend, keep it short
rules.without: Generic, long-winded answers that miss how I work

rules.rule: My defaults: TypeScript, Next.js, check the lockfile, no auto-commit
rules.without: It picks random tools and commits without asking

rules.rule: Where my projects live and what each one is
rules.without: It can't find or understand my work

rules.rule: Links out to WORKFLOW, SECURITY and DESIGN
rules.without: None of the rules load and the standards are ignored

files.risk: the AI starts every project blind and ignores your standards.

files.name: SECURITY.md
files.does: 21 rules so the AI builds safely by default.

rules.rule: Rate-limit every endpoint (login: 5 tries per 15 minutes)
rules.without: Bots brute-force logins and hammer your API

rules.rule: Never hardcode secrets, rotate them if one leaks
rules.without: Your API key sits in Git for anyone to grab and use

rules.rule: Validate and sanitize all input (Zod or Pydantic)
rules.without: Malformed or malicious input crashes the app or injects code

rules.rule: Protect every paid-API route: sign in, rate limit, cap usage
rules.without: A stranger runs up your AI bill on an open URL

rules.rule: Sessions in signed httpOnly cookies, re-checked server-side
rules.without: A copied link or forged cookie logs someone in as you

files.risk: leaked API keys, abused endpoints, surprise bills, data leaks.

files.name: WORKFLOW.md
files.does: How the AI should work on my projects.

rules.rule: Branch off main, never edit main directly
rules.without: A half-finished change auto-deploys straight to production

rules.rule: Read the project's docs before touching anything
rules.without: It re-breaks things the docs already warned about

rules.rule: Run React Doctor on React apps before shipping
rules.without: AI-introduced state and effect bugs ship unnoticed

rules.rule: Leave a handoff in progress.md before any restart
rules.without: You lose all context and re-derive everything next time

rules.rule: Safe deploys: health-check first, instant rollback
rules.without: One bad build takes the live site down with no quick way back

files.risk: agents edit main, break auto-deploys, lose context between sessions.

files.name: DESIGN.md
files.does: How everything should look and feel.

rules.rule: No emojis in the UI, use Lucide icons instead
rules.without: The UI looks AI-generated and unprofessional

rules.rule: No text dashes or arrows, use a middot or an icon
rules.without: Small tells that cheapen the interface

rules.rule: Design UI-first, toward one clear feeling
rules.without: A backend-shaped UI with no real experience
Users stare at a 10 to 30 second spinner

rules.rule: Accessibility: contrast, visible focus, full keyboard use
rules.without: People with low vision or no mouse can't use it

topics.note: The files live in ~/.claude/. CLAUDE.md is the index that ties WORKFLOW.md, SECURITY.md and DESIGN.md together.
